abstract: Intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) lack a stable three-dimensional structure, yet they mediate many of the interactions and regulatory functions of proteins. Alternative splicing produces multiple protein isoforms from a single gene, and because individual exons can encode all or part of an IDR, splicing has the potential to add, remove or reshape disordered regions. However, it remains unclear whether splicing preferentially acts on disordered sequence in all kinds of proteins, how it changes an IDR from one isoform to another, and how this relationship arose during evolution. Here, we map predicted disorder onto the coding exons and genomic codons of human protein isoforms, which allows any two isoforms of a gene to be compared directly, and analyze this map across protein classes and families. We find that alternatively spliced exons are more disordered than constitutive exons in every class of protein, from transcription factors to metabolic enzymes, and that splicing usually changes IDRs at their ends, adding or removing disordered segments as modular units rather than cutting through them. The disordered sequence that splicing varies is compositionally distinct from the disorder that all isoforms share. Notably, the apparent loss of disorder over gene evolution reflects differences between protein families rather than change within them, whereas exons whose splice sites are conserved in few mammals encode more disorder than the other exons of the same gene, with a composition resembling that of young genes. Our results suggest that alternative splicing treats intrinsic disorder as a modular, evolvable layer of protein architecture, and that exons with poorly conserved splice sites may be one route by which disordered sequence enters proteins.
